# RFC-0003: Scheduled parameterized loops

> **Version:** 0.1.0 | **Status:** draft | **Phase:** spec
> **Owners:** @Will Eaton

---

## 1. Summary

### [RFC-0003:C-SCOPE] Scope (Informative) <a id="rfc-0003c-scope"></a>

Two dispatch shapes exist today. A playbook is parameterized, schedulable, and one-shot: it fans a declared graph out over discovered work and reaches a verdict once. A loop iterates propose, apply, measure and decide against a broker-mediated objective, and is dispatched when an issue reaches a scope.

Neither covers recurring work whose answer is a measurement rather than a report. Maintaining a wire contract against an upstream that moves daily is the motivating case: for each supported version line, iterate patches until a conformance objective passes or the attempt is exhausted, then pick up only the drift that arrived since the last firing.

This RFC specifies the missing quadrant: a loop that carries declared parameters, can be launched from a schedule, and advances dedupe state on its own verdict. It does not introduce a new execution machine. It generalizes three things that are presently spelled for playbooks alone: parameter binding, recurrence, and cursor advance.

Out of scope: the objective grammar a loop measures against, which C-MEASURE already governs; and the broker's tool surface, except where a contract must travel with a pack rather than a deployment.

*Since: v0.1.0*

---

## 2. Specification

### [RFC-0003:C-LOOP-PARAMS] Parameters on a loop dispatch (Normative) <a id="rfc-0003c-loop-params"></a>

A pack whose workflow is a loop MAY declare parameters under the same block C-PLAYBOOK-PARAMS governs, with the same literal-only, introspectable-without-evaluation guarantees. The declaration MUST be readable by the same command that reads a playbook's, so that one schema serves both a generated launch form and command-line validation regardless of dispatch shape.

Parameter values MUST be bound before the loop's first turn, and the bound values MUST be frozen for the life of the run: an iteration MUST NOT observe a different value than the iteration before it, so that a measurement is attributable to the candidate rather than to a moved input.

A parameter value that did not originate inside the pack MUST reach an agent prompt only inside a region marked as external input, exactly as C-PLAYBOOK-PARAMS requires. The loop's additional turns do not relax this: every turn that renders a parameter MUST mark it.

The engine MUST reject a parameter declaration on a loop pack that names a value the loop's dispatch cannot bind, rather than binding it silently at the first turn and leaving later turns unparameterized.

*Since: v0.1.0*

### [RFC-0003:C-LOOP-SCHEDULE] Recurrence over a loop (Normative) <a id="rfc-0003c-loop-schedule"></a>

A schedule MUST be able to name a loop pack as its target, with the same cron expression, zone, frozen parameter values and ceilings a playbook schedule carries. The launcher MUST authorize a scheduled loop firing exactly as it authorizes an ad-hoc one: against the pack's stored parameter schema at the digest the schedule was created against, refusing a firing whose schema has drifted rather than launching under values nobody reviewed.

A firing MUST NOT start while a previous firing of the same schedule is still running. A loop occupies substrate for the length of its iterations, so overlapping firings would contend for the same measurement capacity and make each other's results unattributable. The launcher MUST skip rather than queue, and MUST record the skip.

A schedule MUST carry the same ceilings a loop dispatch requires, including the iteration bound. A recurring loop with no iteration bound is unbounded spend on a timer.

The consecutive-failure disable that governs playbook schedules MUST govern loop schedules identically: a schedule whose pack no longer compiles, or whose ceilings no longer render, MUST leave the rotation rather than fail every window forever.

*Since: v0.1.0*

### [RFC-0003:C-LOOP-CURSOR] Cursor advance on a loop verdict (Normative) <a id="rfc-0003c-loop-cursor"></a>

A loop schedule MAY declare a cursor, naming the result path whose scalar advances and the parameter that carries it into the next firing, under the same grammar a playbook schedule uses.

The cursor MUST advance only on a terminal verdict that means the window was actually processed. A loop that exhausted its iterations without reaching its objective MUST NOT advance: the drift it failed to absorb is precisely what the next firing must see again. A loop that reached its objective, and a loop that proved the window needs no change, both MUST advance.

A result carrying no scalar at the declared path MUST leave the cursor where it is and say so on the event log, rather than advancing to a null and silently skipping a window.

An ad-hoc launch MUST NOT advance a schedule's cursor unless it was explicitly opted in and names that schedule, so that a manual investigation cannot eat the next scheduled firing's inputs.

A loop's verdict MUST reach the launcher through the same ingest a one-shot uses. Where a dispatch publishes no terminal event, the launcher MUST treat the run as incomplete and MUST NOT advance; an absent verdict is not a passing one.

*Since: v0.1.0*

### [RFC-0003:C-PACK-CONTRACT] A measurement contract travels with the pack (Normative) <a id="rfc-0003c-pack-contract"></a>

A loop measures through a broker-mediated tool surface. Today the contract that describes that surface is configured per deployment, so a pack cannot be launched anywhere its contract has not been installed by an operator, and two packs cannot disagree about what a measurement means.

A pack that declares a loop workflow MUST be able to declare the contract it measures against, by name and by shape, as part of the pack. The launcher MUST resolve a launch against the contract the pack declares at the rev it was registered at, so that a measurement is reproducible from the frozen artifact alone.

A deployment MUST retain the ability to refuse a declared contract it cannot satisfy, and MUST refuse at launch with a reason naming the substrate it lacks, rather than at the first measurement turn. Ceilings on a contract's cost remain the deployment's: a pack MUST NOT be able to raise the call, wall-clock or accelerator bounds an operator set.

A declared contract MUST NOT widen what a task may reach. It names the tools a turn may call and their parameters; it does not grant access the pack's substrate would otherwise deny.

*Since: v0.1.0*
